answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for a DocumentDB/Cosmos account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. (If deploying MongoDB-specific child resources the ARM path is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/{accountName}/mongodbDatabases and Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/{accountName}/mongodbCollections.)

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in Cosmos DB CLI group: az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create -g myRg -n myAccount --locations regionName=westus2 --kind MongoDB. This is part of the core az CLI (no extension required for basic account management).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (example Bicep: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: accountName ... }). To create MongoDB databases/collections under the account you can use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and /mongodbCollections. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account for the account, plus azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for MongoDB API DBs/collections (examples: resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "my" kind = "MongoDB" ... }).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical connection string (embedded username/password) for Cosmos DB Mongo API: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Example (concrete): mongodb://myUser:mySecretPassword@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. The client must use TLS/SSL (ssl=true) and commonly sets replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false for Cosmos compatibility. Some clusters also accept mongodb+srv:// variants pointing at <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (support can vary).

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB is billed by provisioned throughput measured in Request Units (RUs/sec) or via autoscale RUs and has a serverless mode; throughput can be provisioned at container or database scope. (Note: some dedicated/multi-tenant Mongo offerings may expose vCore-like SKUs, but the standard Cosmos DB model is RU-based billing.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Mongo API for Cosmos DB primarily uses MongoDB credentials (username/password, SCRAM). There is no general Microsoft Entra ID (AAD) authentication for the MongoDB wire protocol — drivers authenticate using the MongoDB URI with the DB user and password (or an account primary key). For other Cosmos DB APIs (SQL) Azure AD is supported, but for Mongo API you should plan to use database users / connection string credentials.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., pymongo or motor for async Python). There is no separate service-specific MongoDB SDK; Cosmos DB has its own SDKs for SQL/Cosmos API, but for the MongoDB-compatible endpoint you use the official MongoDB drivers/ODMs (Beanie/Motor, pymongo, mongoose, etc.).

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Vector-capable clusters (newer MongoDB 7.0-compatible endpoints) support index types like HNSW, IVF and DiskANN (cluster-dependent). The index is created with createIndex on the vector field and vector-specific options. Example (Mongo shell / pymongo style): db.reviews.createIndex( { embedding: "knn" }, { knnVersion: 1, dimensions: 1536, similarity: "cosine", indexOptions: { indexType: "HNSW", m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } } ). (Exact option names can vary by provider; this is the concrete form I'd use to try.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Options: 1) Use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({textField: 'text'})) for basic full-text. 2) For richer/full featured search or hybrid vector+text search, integrate with Azure Cognitive Search (index documents from Cosmos DB) or perform a two-step query in-app (vector nearest-neighbours then filter/rank with text scoring). Cosmos DB Mongo API does not provide Atlas Search; use Azure Cognitive Search or application-side hybrid ranking.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Target cluster in the sample supports the MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol (the newer MongoDB server compatibility). Historically Cosmos Mongo API lagged behind upstream MongoDB; common limitations include differences in transaction semantics, partial support for some aggregation stages and special admin commands, and missing server-side features like certain change-stream options or server-side JavaScript. Expect to test any advanced MongoDB 7.0 feature before relying on it. (For this sample, assume compatibility with MongoDB 7.0 APIs except for a few provider-specific omissions.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full local emulator for the Cosmos DB Mongo API. For local development use the official MongoDB Docker image (e.g., mongo:7.0) and bind to port 27017: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7.0. Adjust connection string to mongodb://localhost:27017. If you must test Cosmos-specific behavior, run against a live Azure cluster (no local emulator available for Mongo API).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB has a Change Feed for its native (SQL) API; the MongoDB change streams feature may be unsupported or limited on some Cosmos Mongo endpoints. If you need change notifications, prefer the Cosmos DB change feed or test the MongoDB change streams behaviour on the target cluster; some clusters require specific server version / feature gates. For safety assume change streams may not be fully supported unless verified on the target cluster.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server (service-specific) to work with this database endpoint. The general azure MCP server does not provide the documentdb-specific inspection/agent features; the documentdb MCP server is the one that has the data-plane tools and index/collection inspectors for the Mongo/DocumentDB service.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft's original managed JSON DB offering was called Azure DocumentDB; it was later rebranded and expanded as Azure Cosmos DB. "DocumentDB" as used historically by Microsoft refers to the SQL API within Cosmos; the MongoDB-compatible service is one API surface of Cosmos DB. This is distinct from any unrelated open-source project also named DocumentDB. In short: Azure DocumentDB -> evolved into Azure Cosmos DB; the Mongo API is a compatibility layer on top of the Cosmos engine.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is Azure Cosmos DB's distributed storage/engine with a MongoDB-compatible wire-protocol translator for the Mongo API; it is not the upstream MongoDB server. That means most MongoDB client code works, but there are behavioral differences (indexing, RU costs, some aggregation stages, transaction semantics, change feed vs change streams) you must validate against the target cluster.

answers.question: What database name should this sample use?
answers.answer: Use database name: sample_retail_07 (create and use only this DB).

answers.question: Where does the sample read the cluster connection string from?
answers.answer: Read the full MongoDB connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. Do not hard-code credentials; use DOCUMENTDB_URI or a config file that references it.

answers.question: What indexes should the sample create for the review pipeline?
answers.answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field and a text index on the review text. Example commands: db.reviews.createIndex({ embedding: "knn" }, { knnVersion:1, dimensions:1536, similarity:"cosine", indexOptions:{ indexType:"HNSW", m:16, efConstruction:200 } }) and db.reviews.createIndex({ text: "text", product_id: 1 }). These are the index definitions the sample will attempt to create/verify at startup (actual option names may vary; verify with the cluster's documentdb MCP tools).

answers.question: How will the application authenticate to the cluster in this sample?
answers.answer: The application will use the MongoDB URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI (username/password embedded in the URI) and pass it to Motor (async pymongo) / Beanie. No Microsoft Entra/AAD flow will be used for Mongo API authentication in this sample.

answers.question: What aggregation pipeline will produce the summary grouped by product and sentiment?
answers.answer: Example aggregation (pymongo syntax): [ { "$group": { "_id": { "product_id": "$product_id", "sentiment": "$sentiment" }, "count": { "$sum": 1 }, "avgSentimentScore": { "$avg": "$sentiment_score" } } }, { "$sort": { "_id.product_id": 1, "count": -1 } } ]. Use collection.aggregate(pipeline) to produce the grouped summary.
